summary: Describes the format of a request to a Time Stamping Authority and of its response, and sets security requirements for how a TSA handles requests.

plainLanguage.summary: It's like asking a trusted clerk to stamp a paper with the date so you can prove when it existed.

questions: how to get a trusted timestamp
what is a time stamping authority
subtitle: A request and response format for getting a trusted authority to sign proof that data existed before a given time.

tldr.problem: A digital signature or a log entry is hard to trust later unless there is proof it already existed at a particular time, for example before a certificate was revoked.
tldr.mechanism: A client sends a Time Stamping Authority (TSA) a hash of its data. The TSA signs a token containing that hash, a trustworthy time and a unique serial number, and sends it back for the client to verify.
tldr.outcome: The token is evidence that the data existed before the stated time without the TSA ever seeing the data. RFC 3161 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 5816.

today: RFC 3161 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 5816. Nothing in the unit metadata says it has been obsoleted.

sections.title: What a Time-Stamping Authority Is For
sections.content:
A time-stamping service supports proof that a datum existed before a particular time. A Time Stamping Authority (TSA) is a Trusted Third Party that provides this proof-of-existence for a datum at an instant in time. It may also be run inside an organization for its own needs.

The RFC's main example is verifying that a digital signature was applied before the matching certificate was revoked, which lets a revoked public key certificate still be used to verify signatures made earlier. A TSA can also record the time of submission when a deadline matters, or the time of entries in a log. An annex shows how to prove a signature was made during a certificate's validity period.

The document does not set overall security requirements for running a TSA, in the same way other PKIX standards do not do so for a CA. Instead, a TSA is expected to publish the policies it follows, and clients should use it only if those policies meet their needs.
sections.plainLanguage: A trusted clerk can tell the world that a paper was shown to them on a certain day. Later nobody can claim the paper was made after that day.

sections.title: What the TSA Must Do
sections.content:
The TSA is REQUIRED to use a trustworthy source of time, put a trustworthy time and a unique integer in each token, and include an identifier of the security policy it was created under. It produces a token on a valid request when it is possible.

Privacy is built in. The TSA time-stamps only a hash of the datum, called a data imprint, tied to a one-way collision resistant hash function identified by an OID. It checks that the hash length fits the algorithm but does not examine the imprint in any other way, and it does not put any identification of the requester in the token.

Each token is signed with a key generated exclusively for this purpose, and the certificate says so. The certificate MUST contain exactly one extended key usage extension with the value id-kp-timeStamping, and that extension MUST be critical. A TSA may hold several keys, for example for different policies or algorithms. If a requester asks for an extension the TSA does not support, the TSA SHALL respond with an error.
sections.plainLanguage: The clerk has a special pen used only for time stamps, never looks at what your paper says, and never writes your name on the stamp.

sections.title: Request, Response and Token Formats
sections.content:
The exchange is two messages. The client sends a TimeStampReq and the TSA answers with a TimeStampResp. The request has a version (v1), a messageImprint (hash algorithm plus the hash value) and optional fields: reqPolicy, nonce, certReq (default false) and extensions. The hash length MUST match the algorithm, for example 20 bytes for SHA-1 or 16 bytes for MD5. If the TSA does not recognize the algorithm or knows it is weak, it SHOULD refuse with bad_alg.

The nonce is a large random number, for example a 64 bit integer, which lets a client check timeliness when it has no local clock. If it is sent, the same value MUST come back. If certReq is true, the TSA's certificate MUST be included in the response, otherwise the certificates field MUST NOT be present.

The response holds a PKIStatusInfo and an optional TimeStampToken. With status zero (granted) or one (grantedWithMods) a token MUST be present, and with any other value it MUST NOT be. Other status values are rejection (2), waiting (3), revocationWarning (4) and revocationNotification (5). When a request fails, failInfo gives the reason, such as badAlg, badRequest, badDataFormat, timeNotAvailable, unacceptedPolicy, unacceptedExtension, addInfoNotAvailable or systemFailure.

The token is a CMS ContentInfo that encapsulates signed data, and it MUST NOT carry any signature other than the TSA's. The signed content is a DER-encoded TSTInfo with these fields:

  • policy, which must equal the requested policy if one was sent, otherwise an unacceptedPolicy error is returned.
  • messageImprint, which must equal the one in the request.
  • serialNumber, unique for each token from a given TSA even after a crash. Users MUST be ready for integers up to 160 bits.
  • genTime, in UTC, written like 19990609001326.34352Z.
  • Optional accuracy (seconds, millis, micros), ordering, nonce, tsa name hint and extensions.

Adding the accuracy to genTime gives an upper bound on when the token was created, and subtracting it gives a lower bound. Unless ordering is true, two tokens can be ordered by genTime only when they differ by more than the sum of their accuracies.
sections.plainLanguage: You hand over a fingerprint of your paper plus a random number. The clerk gives back a signed slip with the same fingerprint, the same random number, the time and a slip number that is never reused.

sections.title: Checking the Response
sections.content:
When the response arrives, the requester SHALL check the status. If there is no error, it SHALL check the token's fields and the validity of its signature. In particular it must confirm that the token holds the correct TSA certificate identifier, the correct data imprint and the correct hash algorithm OID.

It must then verify timeliness, either by comparing the time in the response with a trusted local time reference, or by comparing the nonce in the response with the one it sent. If any check fails, the token SHALL be rejected. Because the TSA's certificate may have been revoked, the requester SHOULD also check its status, for example in the appropriate CRL, and SHOULD check that the policy field is acceptable for the application.
sections.plainLanguage: When the slip comes back you check that it shows your own fingerprint and your own random number, that the signature is real, and that the clerk is still trusted.

sections.title: Transports
sections.content:
No transport is mandatory. The RFC describes four optional ways to carry the messages:

  • E-mail: MIME objects of type application/timestamp-query and application/timestamp-reply, base64-encoded, with file extensions .TSQ and .TSR.
  • Files: a file holds only the DER encoding of one message. Requests SHOULD use .tsq and responses SHOULD use .tsr.
  • TCP sockets: a listener on IP port 318 exchanges messages made of a 32-bit length, an 8-bit flag and a value. The flags cover a plain TSA message, poll replies and requests with a polling reference, partial and final replies, and error text. This lets a client poll for a result that is not ready yet.
  • HTTP: the same two MIME types are used, and a server MUST answer a valid request with either a valid response or an HTTP error.
sections.plainLanguage: You can send your fingerprint by mail, on a file, over a direct line to the clerk's office, or through a web page. The clerk's slip comes back the same way.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC notes that the whole document concerns security, and then lists points that affect trust in a token:

  • Retiring a TSA: if its key is not compromised, the certificate SHALL be revoked. With a reasonCode of unspecified, affiliationChanged, superseded or cessationOfOperation, earlier tokens remain valid. Without a reasonCode, all tokens signed with that key are invalid, so using a reasonCode is recommended.
  • Key compromise: the certificate SHALL be revoked and tokens signed with that key cannot be trusted. An audit trail of tokens, or two tokens from two different TSAs, can help tell real from backdated tokens.
  • Key lifetime: the signing key MUST be long enough for a long life but still has a finite lifetime, so tokens SHOULD be time-stamped again or notarized later to renew trust.
  • Delays: a client using only a nonce and no local clock should treat a response that takes too long as suspect, since a man-in-the-middle can add delay.
  • Linkability: identical data hashed with the same algorithm gives identical imprints, so an observer could infer that tokens refer to the same data.
  • Replays: using a nonce always detects replays and is RECOMMENDED. An alternative is a local clock and a moving time window in which the requester remembers all hashes it sent.
sections.plainLanguage: The slip is only as good as the clerk's special pen. If the pen is lost or stolen, slips can be faked, so there are rules for taking the pen out of use and for getting old slips stamped again.

sections.title: Using Tokens with Signatures
sections.content:
Appendix A defines a Signature Time-stamp attribute for CMS, stored as an unsigned attribute, with the OID id-aa-timeStampToken. The imprint in the token is a hash of the signature field of the SignerInfo being time-stamped.

Appendix B walks through placing a signature at a point in time. The signature is sent to the TSA soon after it is made, and the token is verified. Later the verifier checks that the TSA's time lies within the signer certificate's validity period. Then it fetches the certificate's revocation information as of that time, and if the certificate was revoked, the revocation must be later than the TSA's time. If all this holds, the signature is declared valid.
sections.plainLanguage: Get your signed paper stamped right away. Later, if someone says your pen was stolen, you can show the stamp proves you signed before that happened.
